extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media, comedy, and fact-checking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing autobiographical standup/comedic storytelling with respect to factual accuracy, ethical treatment of real people, and when emotional truth may be prioritized. Focuses on standards for fact-checking, sourcing, and transparency in comedy that claims to be 'true.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy required from comics telling true stories
rubrics_metrics.description: How much accuracy is required from comics who say they are telling true stories about racism, social issues and real people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames this as a central question when comedians present material as factual; evaluators should consider whether claimed events and character portrayals are supported by corroboration and whether claims materially misrepresent real people's actions or motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political comedy: facts come first
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the format is overtly political (e.g., news/analysis comedy shows), factual accuracy is expected to be prioritized over narrative embellishment; factual claims should be verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic storytelling: emotions come first
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In personal storytelling or standup specials, comedians may prioritize emotional truth or narrative effect; evaluators should weigh the importance of literal accuracy versus conveyed emotional reality depending on genre/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful reporting and fact-checking standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our piece... was carefully reported and fact-checked. It is based on interviews with more than 20 people, including former Patriot Act and Daily Show staffers; members of Minhaj's security team; and people who have been the subject of his standup work..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic evaluation expects corroboration from multiple independent sources and fact-checking; allegations about a performer's truthfulness should be supported by interviews, documentation, and cross-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence and context for alleged exaggerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics should present evidence and context to explain why they may have exaggerated elements in their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a performer claims embellishment for effect, they should supply contemporaneous evidence or contextual information that clarifies intent and distinguishes between exaggeration and fabrication; failing to do so invites journalistic scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use documentary evidence to support contested claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing emails and text messages between parties to support one's account (e.g., to show the nature of a friendship or the timing of events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentary records (texts, emails, messages) are persuasive corroboration for disputed autobiographical details and should be used to substantiate timelines and interactions when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inventing or fabricating details to center oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: "Minhaj has elided or concocted other details in his stories, often to place himself more squarely at the center of the action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should not invent scenes, people, or motives that materially misrepresent events to aggrandize themselves; such fabrications harm credibility and can be refuted by reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about embellishment and apologize when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging embellishments (e.g., "I am sorry for embellishing the story") and offering apologies when those embellishments could have harmed others or public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public admissions of exaggeration and sincere apologies can mitigate harm; transparency about what was dramatized versus literal should be part of ethical storytelling practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social consequences of false or embellished stories
rubrics_metrics.description: False stories about police excess or racism can undermine real stories and movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stories touch on systemic injustice or public-interest topics, creators must consider how inaccuracies may damage credibility of genuine claims and the broader social implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in recounting circumstances and motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts should consistently represent timing, circumstances, and motivations (e.g., whether a prom rejection happened in person days before the dance and whether race was a factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrepancies in basic facts or inferences about others' motives weaken credibility; storytellers should aim for internal consistency or clearly mark when memory or interpretation is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective presentation of information to make a point
rubrics_metrics.description: "Minhaj selectively presents information and embellishes to make a point: exactly what we reported."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective omission or framing that materially alters understanding of events is a form of rhetorical manipulation; ethical practice requires acknowledging omitted context when it would change audience interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish evaluative standards by show/format
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between how factual material is handled in political comedy shows like Patriot Act and in standup specials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should apply different truth standards depending on the format: news-adjacent or political programs demand higher factual fidelity, while personal comedic storytelling may allow for more narrative license—but that license has limits when real people and serious issues are involved.
